REUTERS/Stelios Misinas AGIOS KONSTANTINOS, Greece, Aug 2 (Reuters) - Two firefighting helicopters collided in Greece while helping ⁠to control a huge wildfire on Sunday that has destroyed more than 100 homes northwest of Athens, while people fled another blaze on the tourist island of Kefalonia. Two people on one helicopter — a Greek ⁠and a Danish national — died, while the crew on the other, one person from Greece, one from Britain, survived, the fire service said. Investigations had started into what caused the collision, ‌it added. Europe has been ravaged by wildfires this summer after a period of record-breaking heatwaves and little rain – conditions that scientists say have been exacerbated by climate change. Destructive blazes in France and Spain showed some signs of easing over the weekend, but several wildfires have broken out in Greece after a period of relative calm there. The two helicopters collided in the area of Psatha in the Attica region, Greece's fire service said in a statement. Video posted on the Forecast Weather Greece Facebook page appeared to show two helicopters closing to cross paths at ​low altitude, before the main rotor of the lower helicopter struck the underside of the other. The lower one then crashed in flames. The ⁠second helicopter then dumped its load of water and flew away. Reuters has not ⁠verified the authenticity of the footage. Investigations suggested the fire that started in the Greek region of Boeotia before spreading to Attica was caused by sparks from conductors on a private network transmitting electricity generated by wind ⁠turbines ‌to the main power grid, the eKathimerini website reported. Two Greek nationals were arrested on suspicion of negligence, while another suspect remains at large, the report said. 'FORCE OF NATURE' Gale-force winds that had fuelled a fire around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth 60 km (40 miles) northwest of Athens subsided, but flames crossed a mountain to the south and reached the settlement of Veniza and a military firing range, igniting unexploded ordnance. Emergency crews focused their ⁠efforts on preventing fire from advancing towards the coastal town of Megara, which has a population of around 30,000. "There are ​moments when the force of nature and the intensity of weather conditions ‌exceed all human planning and every operational capability,” Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in his regular Sunday message. Greek authorities issued emergency alerts for evacuations for a number of settlements in western Attica, including ⁠an industrial estate near Megara. In the ​village of Agios Konstantinos, residents were doing their best to halt the spread of the blaze. "The fire has been burning since last night, it is certain that they cannot have forces everywhere. We as residents are doing everything we can,” said Tasos Tzempelikos, 61, who along with his son was pouring water on the fire. Overnight, several settlements on the Ionian island of Kefalonia were evacuated after a fire broke out in the Pastra area in the south. FIRE IN FRANCE CHANGES COURSE In France, a fire in the southwestern Var ⁠region switched direction after a change in the wind and surged into a forested area that was difficult to access, ​BFM TV reported. A new fire also broke out alongside a highway near the historic southern city of Carcassonne, apparently caused by a blazing vehicle, BFM TV added. Video on the channel showed huge plumes of billowing grey smoke and flames near the road. Authorities said they had closed the highway and evacuated a nearby animal park. In Montfort-sur-Argens in Var, Georges Blanc, who had fled the fire earlier, returned home and was busy putting out hot embers to prevent a flare-up, while ⁠firefighters watered the wider area. "With the combined efforts of the two Canadairs (firefighting planes) and the firefighters, I think you could say all the houses were saved ... And now, well, I'm coming back to check, because since I saw the flames, I thought the houses wouldn't have survived," he told Reuters. In central Spain, wildfires that ripped through tens of thousands of hectares over the past week were mostly under control, though firefighters were dealing with reignitions in some areas. In the western province of Caceres, a forest blaze erupted on Saturday, prompting the evacuation of around 800 people. Those residents were allowed to return on Sunday but remained confined to their homes as the fire was still active. HUNGARY ​NUCLEAR PLANT FORCED TO SHUT Other European countries are struggling with drought and receding water levels in major rivers, including the Rhine and the Danube, which recorded its ⁠lowest-ever water levels in Hungary, Serbia and Romania. Hungary faces a critical five days, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, as the drying out of the Danube forced the country's sole nuclear power plant to shut for the first time ​in more than four decades, with a new heatwave looming. Falls in water levels amid a lack of rain have also disrupted shipping and tourism ‌in Hungary and triggered water-use restrictions in more than 100 cities and villages. Danube levels in Serbia fell to ​their lowest since 1985, cutting the daily output of the country's biggest hydropower plant to only 20%, the energy minister said on Sunday. (Reporting by Aleksandar Vasovic in Belgrade, Dominique Patton in Paris, Manon Cruz and Fatos Bytyci in Var, Gergely Szakacs in Budapest, Louisa Gouliamaki, Angelos Tsatsis, Vania Turner in Greece, Andrey Khalip in Madrid; Writing by Aleksandar Vasovic; Editing by Christina Fincher, Alex Richardson and Andrew Heavens) Follow us on our official WhatsApp channel for breaking news alerts and key updates! https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwy8.text: Image source, BBC Indonesia Image caption, Ex-headmaster Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, has been accused of sexual abuse By Endang Nurdin ,Â Rebecca Henschke ,Â BBC Eye Investigations Â and Â BBC Indonesia Published 4 hours ago A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report. Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok. Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him , and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities. The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police. Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault Catching My Teacherâ¯ Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in Indonesia Watch on iPlayer Listen on Sounds Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube , external . The student detectives Central to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar. They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school. By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta. Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school. Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school. Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations. In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation. "Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said. Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC. In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent. Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions. Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name". The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases. Figure caption, Watch: BBC tracks down abusive teacher secretly released early More students come forward The day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands. One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter. "I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school." Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married , were overwhelmed by the response from former students. "It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'." Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse. "They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said. Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously. "It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC. Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process. The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time. NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals. In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward. BlaÅ¾io / LRT nuotr. The National Library of Lithuania is currently hosting an exhibition of 150 drawings by the Dutch master Rembrandt. They are facsimiles from a rare portfolio published in 1903, only seven copies of which survive. One is owned by the Lithuanian artist and collector Vaidotas Å½ukas. Below, he explains the meaning and value of the Rembrandt portfolio.Â The works in this exhibition first came into my possession through this very library. During the winter of 1979â1980, I worked in a department of the Republican Library headed by Aleksandras Kubilas (1928â2021), who was not only a librarian but also a collector. He visited the studio I had established in my parentsâ apartment in the Scientistsâ House, across from LukiÅ¡kÄs Prison. Kubilas acquired one of my painted portraits for 300 roubles and gave me this portfolio of Rembrandt drawings. At the time, he also recounted the story of its provenance. The account may be partly a legend, but I know of no other version and have been unable to verify it. According to the former owner, âthe portfolio was taken by the Red Army in 1945 from the Royal University Library in Berlin and transported to Moscow as a trophy of war. At Vilnius railway station, it was exchanged for a litre of moonshine.â Rembrandtâs work has fascinated me since my youth. As a student, I visited the Hermitage in Leningrad and spent several days wandering alone through its Rembrandt galleries. Eventually, the guards were instructed to remove me, perhaps because they suspected that I was planning some mischief. The cover of the portfolio | photo courtesy of V. Å½ukas The paradoxes of the collectionâs survival It is noteworthy that Rembrandt himself assembled an extensive collection whose fate is highly revealing. We know its contents only because he fell deeply into debt and was declared bankrupt. Notaries inventoried his large Amsterdam house and its entire collection before the property was sold at an auction. In that sense, even misfortune can leave a valuable historical record. The notarial inventory shows that Rembrandt owned dozens of turbans and hundreds of feathers, horns, and claws brought by ship from Africa, India, the Middle East, and the Far East. His home was, in effect, a storehouse of authentic props. Several items from this collection appear in the drawings exhibited here, including a two-handed sword, armour, and figures wearing turbans. Rembrandt's drawings exhibited at the National Library of Lithuania | LRT TV Rembrandt also collected dried marine specimens, including coral, starfish, and shells. Other curiosities such as snakes, lizards, molluscs, and unfamiliar fish were preserved in jars of alcohol. He owned taxidermized animals of various sizes, as well as an extensive collection of weapons: cannons, crossbows, helmets, and daggers. His holdings also included portrait busts of all the Roman emperors. By comparison, the Antwerp painter Peter Paul Rubens owned original antique busts, which he later sold to English aristocrats, whereas Rembrandt was satisfied with high-quality copies. He approached the artistic heritage of earlier periods in a similar manner. Although he travelled little â he had a family and worked prolifically â his chests contained engravings after many earlier European masters, giving him a broad understanding of artistic developments in Germany, Spain, and Italy. Several original paintings by Raphael nevertheless hung in his house. He also amassed fabrics, belts, saddles, harnesses, and jewellery, including gold and pearl necklaces, brooches, rings, and bracelets. Why did he need all those objects? I believe the answer lies in his art. He painted his wife, Saskia, seated on his lap, dressed in sumptuous velvet and wearing a jewelled diadem. In a self-portrait, Rembrandt depicts himself laughing, holding a tall glass of wine, with an ornate sword at his belt. The Prodigal Son in the Brothel, a self-portrait with Saskia by Rembrandt van Rijn, 1635 His biblical King Solomon, also represented in one of the drawings in this exhibition, is clothed in soft furs. In Rembrandtâs painting of a Polish horseman, now in the Frick Collection in New York, the rider wears gold-trimmed boots, red Polish trousers, and a red cap edged with sable. He carries a bow, a quiver filled with arrows, a battle axe, and several swords; the horse is fitted with elaborate bridles and precious stirrups. Such ethnographic detail appears throughout Rembrandtâs drawings, etchings, and paintings, yet it never becomes mere illustration. The master understood the restraint and distance required for art to remain art rather than descend into idle display. A murderer from Denmark While preparing this exhibition, I consulted numerous documents preserved in the archives of Leiden and Amsterdam, with online translation tools proving invaluable. The exhibition at the Martynas MaÅ¾vydas National Library includes two drawings in which Rembrandt depicts a woman tied to a post, perhaps still alive, perhaps already dead. They were clearly drawn from life: one shows the figure from the front and the other from the side. In both, an axe is fastened to the crossbar. Elsje Christiaens after her execution, two drawings by Rembrandt van Rijn, 1664 The documents later revealed that the woman was Elsje Christiaens, an eighteen-year-old from Jutland, Denmark. After arriving in Amsterdam, she found work as a domestic servant. Following a dispute with her landlady, she was killed with an axe. The case was thoroughly documented because women convicted of murder were rare in Amsterdam. Christiaens was publicly executed on Dam Square in accordance with Dutch law. Her body was then taken to a site in the wetlands north of Amsterdam known as the Gallows Field. Among the surviving records associated with Rembrandt is a receipt for a boat hired to reach that location. Other Dutch artists also depicted this execution ground and the bodies of condemned prisoners displayed there. Earlier scholars dated Rembrandtâs drawings of the condemned woman to 1655. The Dutch historian Isabella van Eeghen (1913â1996), however, discovered records of the crime in the Amsterdam City Archives that established the later date of 1664. She wrote: âThe fate of Elsje Christiaens was intended as a warning against crime; now it will serve as a warning to art historians to be cautious when dating works solely on stylistic grounds.â Prof. ArÅ«nas Sverdiolas examines drawings from Rembrandt's portfolio | photo courtesy of V. Å½ukas Will restitution take place? The portfolio of Rembrandt drawings currently exhibited at the National Library in Vilnius is a bibliographic treasure. It was printed in The Hague in 1903 using heliography, a rare and costly reproduction process at the time. Bearing the stamps of the Royal University Library in Berlin, the portfolio is numbered 7. Publicly available information indicates that only six comparable portfolios of Rembrandt drawings are held in the United States, all in museums and university libraries in New York and other cities. Fifty drawings from this portfolio were exhibited ten years ago as part of the SantaraâÅ viesa Congress programme at the Alanta Manor Gallery, and again during the winter of 2018â2019 at the Gothic House of PerkÅ«nas, then home to the Institute of Life and Faith. At the opening of the Alanta exhibition in 2016, Leonidas Donskis introduced the works from the portfolio. Rembrandt's drawing stamp | photo courtesy of V. Å½ukas After the event, Irena VeisaitÄ, Elena BradÅ«naitÄ, and Leonidas Donskis asked what I intended to do with it. I replied that I wished to show it to the public in Vilnius and then return it to the Berlin library. All agreed, while emphasising that the return should not take place without public attention. For several years, working through the Lithuanian Embassy in Berlin, we have sought sources and documents that could substantiate the alleged theft in 1945. If such evidence is found, the restitution process can begin. LRT English Newsletter Every Friday morning. Thanks for subscribing!
